about.name: Monero
about.what: A cryptocurrency private by default: sender, receiver and amount are hidden on its blockchain.
about.thesis: Holders value it as digital cash with strong financial privacy built in for every user, not as an optional feature.
about.risk: Privacy coins face exchange delistings and regulatory pressure in several countries, which limits access and liquidity.

about.name: Solana
about.what: A high-throughput proof-of-stake blockchain for apps, payments and trading; SOL pays fees and is staked to secure it.
about.thesis: Holders see it as the high-speed chain for on-chain markets: low fees, one of the busiest trading and memecoin ecosystems, and growing use for payments.
about.risk: Past network outages and stiff competition from other chains could slow adoption; much activity is speculative trading.

about.name: Bitcoin
about.what: The first cryptocurrency: a public payment network and digital asset with a fixed cap of 21 million coins.
about.thesis: Holders see it as digital gold: a fixed 21M supply, the deepest crypto market, and growing use as a reserve asset by ETFs, companies and governments.
about.risk: Its value rests on belief and adoption alone; it has no cash flows and its price has seen repeated deep drawdowns.

about.name: Zcash
about.what: A cryptocurrency with optional shielded transactions that use zero-knowledge proofs to hide sender, receiver and amount.
about.thesis: Holders see it as Bitcoin-like scarce money (21 million cap) with strong, provable privacy available to users who choose it.
about.risk: Privacy features draw regulatory and exchange-listing pressure, and much use still happens through transparent addresses.

about.name: Tesla, Inc.
about.what: A US maker of electric vehicles, battery energy-storage systems and solar products, also developing self-driving and robots.
about.thesis: The case is that Tesla is an AI and robotics company: self-driving, robotaxis, Optimus robots and energy storage could grow larger than the car business.
about.risk: Much of the valuation rests on unproven autonomy and robotics businesses, while car sales face rising competition.

about.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
about.what: A major US maker of memory and storage chips (DRAM, NAND), including high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators.
about.thesis: Holders see AI driving demand for high-bandwidth memory, where Micron is one of only a few suppliers.
about.risk: Memory is a cyclical commodity business; oversupply can drive sharp price and earnings swings.

about.name: Anonymous Cat
about.what: A Solana memecoin (Anonymous Cat) that airdrops Solana-native ZEC to its holders, funded by a 3% transfer fee.
about.thesis: Holders own it for the airdrops: simply holding ZCAT is meant to earn Solana-native ZEC, on top of any move in the memecoin itself.
about.risk: The airdrops are the project's own claim and not guaranteed; a 3% fee on every transfer and memecoin swings cut into returns.

about.name: Pump.fun
about.what: The token of pump.fun, the largest memecoin launchpad on Solana, where anyone can launch and trade new tokens in a few clicks.
about.thesis: Holders see it as a share in Solana's biggest memecoin launchpad: the platform earns fees and uses part of that revenue to buy PUMP back.
about.risk: Revenue depends on meme-coin trading, which is volatile and faddish; buybacks are a platform policy that can change.

about.name: Sui
about.what: A proof-of-stake smart-contract blockchain built with the Move programming language, designed for fast, parallel transactions.
about.thesis: Holders see it as a newer, high-performance chain whose design suits games, payments and consumer apps, with a growing ecosystem.
about.risk: A large share of supply is still unlocking over time, and it competes with established chains for users and developers.

about.name: NEAR Protocol
about.what: A proof-of-stake smart-contract blockchain that splits work across shards to scale; NEAR pays fees and secures the network by staking.
about.thesis: Holders see it as a scalable, developer-friendly base layer, with recent focus on AI agents and chain abstraction to make apps easier to use.
about.risk: It competes with many larger smart-contract chains for developers and users; adoption, not technology, decides the outcome.

about.name: Hyperliquid
about.what: The native token of Hyperliquid, a blockchain built to run an on-chain order-book exchange, mainly for perpetual futures.
about.thesis: The case is that trading fees from a fast-growing on-chain exchange flow back to the token, largely through buybacks by the protocol's Assistance Fund.
about.risk: Token value depends on exchange volume holding up against rival venues and on the platform avoiding technical or regulatory setbacks.

about.name: Toncoin (The Open Network)
about.what: The native coin of The Open Network, a proof-of-stake blockchain closely integrated with the Telegram messaging app.
about.thesis: Holders see Telegram's very large user base as a built-in distribution channel for payments, wallets and mini-apps running on TON.
about.risk: Growth leans heavily on the Telegram link; any change in that relationship or regulatory pressure on it would hit the case.

about.name: Bittensor
about.what: A blockchain network where independent 'subnets' reward participants in TAO for producing useful machine-learning work.
about.thesis: The case is that an open, incentive-driven market for AI services can grow outside big tech firms, with TAO as the network's reward currency.
about.risk: Measuring the real usefulness of subnet output is hard; rewards may outpace genuine demand for the AI services produced.

about.name: SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust
about.what: An ETF tracking the S&P 500 Index of about 500 large US companies across all sectors.
about.thesis: Holders use it as broad, low-cost exposure to the US stock market as a whole.
about.risk: It falls with the broad US market; the index is increasingly weighted toward its largest companies.

about.name: Invesco QQQ Trust
about.what: An ETF tracking the Nasdaq-100 Index: the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq.
about.thesis: Holders use it as a simple, low-cost way to own the largest US growth and technology companies in one fund.
about.risk: Heavily weighted to a handful of mega-cap tech stocks, so it is less diversified than a broad market fund.

about.name: ARK Innovation ETF
about.what: An actively managed ETF run by ARK Invest that holds companies it views as leaders in disruptive innovation.
about.thesis: Holders want a concentrated, actively picked basket of high-growth innovation companies such as AI, genomics, fintech and autonomy.
about.risk: Concentrated, high-volatility holdings; results depend heavily on the manager's stock picks, which can lag the market.

about.name: Global X Robotics & Artificial Intelligence ETF
about.what: An ETF tracking an index of developed-market companies in robotics and AI, from industrial robots to surgical systems.
about.thesis: Holders want diversified exposure to automation and robotics adoption across factories, healthcare and AI software.
about.risk: Holdings are concentrated in a few large names and sensitive to industrial cycles and tech sentiment.

about.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF
about.what: An exchange-traded fund tracking an index of companies developing or using AI and big-data technology, including hardware makers.
about.thesis: Holders want broad, diversified exposure to the AI theme across many companies instead of picking single stocks.
about.risk: It is concentrated in large tech names, so a broad tech or AI-sentiment downturn hits most holdings at once.

about.name: Marvell Technology, Inc.
about.what: A US chip company designing data-infrastructure semiconductors: custom AI chips, networking, optical and storage.
about.thesis: The case is that cloud providers increasingly want custom AI chips and fast optical links, both core Marvell businesses.
about.risk: Relies on a few large cloud customers whose spending plans or in-house chip choices can shift.

about.name: Astera Labs, Inc.
about.what: A US chip company making connectivity chips and modules that move data between processors, memory and networks in AI data centers.
about.thesis: The case is that AI servers need ever-faster links between chips, and Astera's connectivity products sit inside that build-out.
about.risk: Revenue depends on a small number of large customers and on AI data-center spending staying strong.

about.name: Cerebras Systems Inc.
about.what: A US maker of AI computing systems built around a wafer-scale chip; also sells AI compute as a cloud service. Listed on Nasdaq May 2026.
about.thesis: Holders see it as a challenger taking AI-compute share from NVIDIA with a different approach: one wafer-sized chip instead of clusters of GPUs, built for very fast AI.
about.risk: Newly public, competing with far larger chip makers; revenue has historically leaned on a few large customers.

about.name: IonQ, Inc.
about.what: One of the leading quantum-computing companies: it builds trapped-ion quantum computers, sold through the major clouds and as systems.
about.thesis: Holders see it as a quantum front-runner with real customers, including US Air Force Research Lab contracts, positioned to benefit as quantum computing matures.
about.risk: Commercially useful quantum computing may take years; the company is loss-making and faces well-funded rivals.

about.name: Unusual Machines, Inc.
about.what: A US maker of drone components (flight controllers, FPV cameras, video transmitters, goggles), selling under the Fat Shark and Rotor Riot brands to defense drone builders and hobby pilots.
about.thesis: Holders see it as a domestic supplier filling the gap left by US restrictions on Chinese drone parts, with parts on the Pentagon's Blue UAS list, defense-builder orders and a large cash pile with no debt.
about.risk: Revenue is still small and depends on government drone policy and a few customers; a small, volatile stock where execution, supply and margins can swing hard.
